title: I Gave an AI Agent the Keys to My Life (Here's What Happened) — Radek Sienkiewicz (@velvetshark-com)

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 96%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk describes a personal AI agent harness combining LLMs for judgment, scripts for deterministic tasks, memory files, and overnight automation loops for managing a user's digital life.

summary: Radek Sienkiewicz, an Open Claw maintainer, describes how he incrementally gave an AI agent control over his digital life. Rather than a single big leap, he expanded permissions one step at a time—starting with WhatsApp chat, migrating to Telegram, then Discord—and progressively granting access to emails, notes, files, calendars, tools, and his operating system. This incremental philosophy means when things break, he takes one small step back, fixes it, understands why it failed, and continues forward, avoiding catastrophic failures. A pivotal development was integrating his Obsidian knowledge base of approximately 3,000 markdown pages containing work, personal, tasks, projects, research, articles, and bookmarks. The agent uses normal search, QMD search for Obsidian, and workspace memory, all interlinked. When he adds bookmarks to an inbox, the agent analyzes the content, adds tags and context, finds connections to existing notes, and surfaces relevant prior knowledge he may have forgotten. Overnight automation (roughly 3-6am) handles indexing, backups, refreshing QMD/memory/Obsidian indexes, email and calendar summaries, and Open Claw version updates with protective verification scripts. He identifies three core job types: ambient operations (plumbing, updates), attention filtering (proactive alerts like Netflix payment failures, domain renewals, drafting email replies), and execution support. Discord channels organize these functions into dedicated spaces: general, inbox, consulting, video research, briefing, Instagram, YouTube, open claw, and a playground for testing new configurations. The architecture combines LLMs for judgment with scripts for deterministic tasks, and optimized memory files including soul MD, critical rules MD, and agent MD. He evolved from a single memory file to a memory folder with dreaming and memory promotion. Challenges include bad memory compounding as vaults grow to thousands of notes, brittle multi-step automations that break (mitigated by splitting into simpler ones or adding guardrails), noisy nodes requiring regular cleaning, and weak boundaries requiring optimization of soul MD and related files. Radek's concluding philosophy is to 'optimize for the future self'—treating one's future self as a person to help, with the agent doing as much as possible overnight so that when he wakes up, work is already completed by someone other than himself.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and path to OpenClaw
sections.summary: Radek introduces himself as an Open Claw maintainer and describes how he gave the agent keys to his digital life—access to emails, notes, files, calendars, tools, and operating system—not all at once but step by step.

sections.title: Philosophy of incremental growth and system updates
sections.summary: Radek explains his incremental approach: starting with WhatsApp, migrating to Telegram, then Discord, adding one simple workflow at a time. When something breaks, he takes one small step back, fixes it, and continues. This philosophy also led him to become a maintainer through submitting PRs. He discovered his 'simple' setup is more sophisticated than most others' configurations.

sections.title: Integrating the Obsidian knowledge base
sections.summary: Radek integrated his Obsidian vault of ~3,000 markdown pages (work, personal, tasks, projects, research, articles) with Open Claw using normal search, QMD search, and workspace memory. When he adds bookmarks to an inbox, the agent analyzes content, adds tags and context, finds connections to existing notes, and surfaces forgotten relevant knowledge. He references Andrej Karpathy's viral tweet about LLM knowledge bases as confirming his setup.

sections.title: Ambient operations and overnight automation
sections.summary: Overnight (roughly 3-6am) the agent indexes everything, backs up data (limiting worst-case loss to a couple hours), refreshes QMD/memory/Obsidian indexes, prepares email and calendar summaries, and updates Open Claw with verification scripts. Radek starts each morning with a fresh, ready system.

sections.title: Core job types for the AI agent
sections.summary: Radek identifies three job types: ambient operations (plumbing, updates, background maintenance), attention filtering (proactively alerting about important emails using Obsidian context—examples include Netflix payment failure fixed in 5 minutes, domain renewal, and drafting project-related replies), and execution support (drafting and synthesizing).

sections.title: Discord integration channels
sections.summary: Radek shows his Discord channel structure: general, inbox (for link-dropping and knowledge base building), consulting (client projects, quotes, deadlines), video research, briefing (morning briefings), Instagram, YouTube, open claw (maintainer work), and a playground channel for testing new models, workspaces, or memory configurations before promoting them.

sections.title: System architecture: LLMs, scripts, and memory management
sections.summary: The architecture combines LLMs for judgment (understanding emails, making connections), scripts for deterministic tasks (skipping LLM entirely when unnecessary), and optimized memory files. Radek uses soul MD, critical rules MD (placed high in agent MD to prevent forgetting), and evolved from a single memory file to a memory folder with dreaming and memory promotion. Everything in Open Cog is inspectable and editable. The section ends introducing bad memory as a challenge.

sections.title: Challenges: Bad memory, brittle automations, noisy nodes, and weak boundaries
sections.summary: Radek details key challenges: bad memory compounds when vaults and memories grow to thousands of notes, requiring active maintenance. Brittle multi-step automations (e.g., 10-step) will break at some point—mitigated by splitting into simpler automations or adding effective guardrails. Noisy nodes require regular cleaning. Weak boundaries necessitate optimizing soul MD and related files for one's needs.

sections.title: Conclusion: Optimizing for the future self
sections.summary: Radek advises starting with one recurring pain, growing trust incrementally, building a knowledge base, moving as much as possible to markdown files, and leveraging Open Claw's inspectability. He closes with the philosophy of optimizing for the future self: past me is lazy, future me is an all-powerful creature—but the job is to befriend and help the future you. The agent's purpose is to help the future me as much as possible overnight, so when Radek wakes up, as much as could be done is already done by someone other than himself.
